skills.when_to_use: Use when the question demands precise cross-video correspondence or discrimination, recognizable from the question text and video list alone: questions that reference labeled object IDs across synchronized camera views and ask where one object is when an event involving another occurs; questions that name a time interval or timestamp in one video and ask for the functionally equivalent step or interval in another; questions asking which of several videos or options exhibits a stated property or error; or questions asking which action is performed incorrectly a stated number of times across videos of the same activity. Do not use for open narrative inference questions (e.g., predicting a middle segment from a beginning and an ending) where summarizing each video separately suffices.
skills.strategy: Apply this procedure in order and let it override the default single-pass workflow. Stage 1, neutral first acquisition: for each referenced video, issue one per-video instruction asking for a timestamped, purely descriptive account of the relevant objects, actions, or scenes (each occurrence with its visible start and end seconds and its visible attributes). Do not embed the answer options, a yes/no verdict request, or an expected conclusion in the first pass, because verdict-seeking instructions bias the analyst toward confirming or denying the premise instead of reporting what is actually visible. For a referenced event at a stated time, request a description of that interval plus several seconds of surrounding context. Stage 2, consistency gate before answering: before submitting any answer, compare all accumulated reports against each other and against the output format the question demands. Raise a flag when: (a) two reports about the same object or moment directly conflict (e.g., one report says an object is not visible while another locates it); (b) a report is null in a way that would make the question unanswerable; (c) a report is degenerate relative to the required answer, such as a single point timestamp where the question requires an interval with distinct start and end, or an event reported to occur only at exactly 0 seconds, or an action described with no visible duration; (d) a report's raw visual description contradicts its own interpretive conclusion (e.g., a weapon at a character's neck is described but the summary concludes no danger, or an action is listed but declared never performed). Stage 3, targeted re-acquisition when flagged: do not answer from flagged evidence and do not guess from assumptions about how such question sets are usually constructed. Instead run one focused follow-up. For identity or position conflicts across synchronized views, use a joint watch of the relevant videos clipped to a short window around the claimed moment, keeping the total selected duration small so sampling stays dense enough to catch brief or fine-grained events; ask the visual model to describe the raw visual layout of the labeled objects at that moment without stating which answer option is correct. For interval answers, request the full visible start and end seconds of the action, including how long it visibly continues after it begins, and require two distinct numbers. For an event that could plausibly occur at a different time than claimed, ask for the complete timeline of candidate occurrences before pinning the interval. Stage 4, final answer from raw description: answer only from the described visual content, not from an analyst's verdict phrase and not from plausibility priors about intended answers. If the question presupposes exactly one correct option but all raw descriptions still fail to support any option, do not select an option merely to satisfy that presupposition through guesswork; choose the option whose support rests on the strongest described visual details, re-read the raw descriptions for a detail that resolves the choice, and record the residual uncertainty in the answer's reason. Never substitute a discussion of missing evidence for the requested answer representation.

skills.when_to_use: The active local instruction asks for visual facts, events, objects, actions, attributes or states in this one video (e.g., what is shown or done, where/when something occurs, how something looks or changes), and the answer must come from the video's visual content rather than metadata such as duration or labels. Use this whenever the instruction names an evidence need that frames can resolve, including when it is one part of a larger multi-video comparison resolved elsewhere.
skills.strategy: First compare the instruction with retained same-video Memory: if Memory already contains observations that directly settle every part of the instruction, finish immediately with a summary of that evidence. Otherwise, or if Memory only partially covers it, plan observations. Turn the instruction into one concrete, visually answerable question per observe action; make it specific enough that a visual model could answer it by watching frames (name the target objects, actions, attributes, or time period of interest). Choose ranges from what the instruction and any retained Memory indicate: when Memory or the instruction points to a likely time region, cover that region narrowly with a comfortable margin around it; when the location of the target event or object is unknown, cover the full duration or large ordered chunks of it, splitting into up to 8 non-overlapping ranges in one action so each region gets its own visual call and its own frame capacity. Pick one planned FPS tied to the evidence need: dense sampling (e.g., 2-25 FPS) for brief, fast, or fine-grained motion and detail; low sampling (e.g., 0.1-2 FPS) for coarse scene content, slow changes, or long spans; each range is capped at 512 frames independently, so a longer range can still be sampled if you accept a lower rate, and Runtime will adjust the effective FPS per range if needed. After each observation arrives as a Memory line, judge whether it answers the instruction: if a detail is still missing, uncertain, or contradicted, issue a further observe with a narrowed range around the promising segment, an adjusted FPS (higher to resolve detail, lower to widen coverage), or a rephrased question targeting exactly the missing detail; keep the objective question phrasing self-contained, since only you see prior context. Do not re-observe segments whose Memory already answers the question. Stop observing and finish once Memory contains the requested facts with usable confidence, or once further observations cannot plausibly change the result (e.g., the whole duration has been covered for the target and it is absent). The finish summary must be self-contained and grounded only in retained observations: state the answer-relevant findings for this instruction in plain language, include where in the video the evidence was seen when it helps the coordinator compare across videos, and state any uncertainty or absence (e.g., target never appears) explicitly, without mentioning observations as tool calls, ranges, FPS values, or planning steps.
